steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper arguing that online HD map estimation from a car's sensors should make use of existing, possibly outdated or inaccurate, maps. Cover the background on autonomous driving and HD maps, our idea and the paper's structure, the contributions and their impact, and the map terminology we use.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous Driving is a complex problem that promises to change a lot how we interact with transportation. Full vehicle automation still seems quite far away, but partially autonomous vehicles are now found on a number of road systems in the world. These vehicles have to process a lot of information to work, from the raw sensor data to elaborate maps of road networks.

High Definition maps (HDMaps) in particular are a crucial component of research on self-driving cars (Fig. 1 shows a few simple examples of maps, with road boundaries as green polylines, lane dividers as lime polylines and pedestrian crossings as blue polygons). Maps are not a typical input for neural networks, but they have necessary information that helps the car understand the world it has to navigate. So a lot of effort has gone into incorporating this new type of data into solutions. These efforts have shown that HDMaps have remarkable benefits, both for fundamental problems like Object Detection and for precise trajectory forecasting problems.

However these maps are expensive to acquire and to maintain, because they need precise data acquisition and exacting human labeling. So there has been a strong push to approximate HDMaps from sensor data. Seminal work showed that even rough estimated maps are useful for trajectory forecasting.

Recent methods like MapTRv2 have become good at generating online HDMaps from raw sensors, but we think they overlook data that is very useful and nearly always available: existing maps. Our position is that outdated or lower quality maps should usually be available and that they significantly improve the estimated HDMaps, as shown in Fig. 1. In fact, even “map-free” models tend to use lower-quality satnav maps, and estimated maps could always be available if a vehicle went through a place once.

In this paper we explore the central postulate that even inaccurate existing maps improve the estimation of HDMaps from raw sensors. After giving some context on our method and the field in Sec. 2, we propose two separate technical contributions: in Sec. 3 we describe reasonable scenarios where an inaccurate map can be available, with practical implementations, and in Sec. 4 we propose MapEX, an architecture that generates HDMaps from sensor data while taking existing map information into account. Last, in Sec. 5 we present results with experiments on the nuScenes dataset.

- Contributions (three)
  - account for existing map info when estimating online HDMaps
  - reasonable scenarios with imperfect existing maps; realistic implementations + code for nuScenes
  - MapEX: query based HDMap estimation; non-learnable existing (EX) queries; pre-attributing predictions to known ground truth correspondences in training

- Impact
  - lowers bar for good, cost-effective maps; noisy/"shifted" element positions: 84.8% mAP, +38% over MapTRv2 base; +8% over state-of-the-art MapNeXt (cite) with foundation model image backbone (cite) vs our ResNet-50
  - more crucial as estimated maps get more complex
  - first to directly integrate existing map matching sensor data location (input sample); blind spot; prior: geolocalized satellite maps (cite), SDMaps (cite), retrieval of similar map from pre-computed database (cite); none use sensors to correct flawed map
  - implementation of three realistic existing map scenarios; both flawed existing + true HDMap per sample; Trust but Verify (cite) map change detection dataset only existing map + change label

- Map nomenclature
  - local 30m\times 60m maps around a sample
  - true maps = ground truth; existing maps = inputs; predicted maps = model estimates

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous Driving is a complex problem that promises to change a lot how we interact with transportation. Full vehicle automation still seems quite far away, but partially autonomous vehicles are now found on a number of road systems in the world. These vehicles have to process a lot of information to work, from the raw sensor data to elaborate maps of road networks.

High Definition maps (HDMaps) in particular are a crucial component of research on self-driving cars (Fig. 1 shows a few simple examples of maps, with road boundaries as green polylines, lane dividers as lime polylines and pedestrian crossings as blue polygons). Maps are not a typical input for neural networks, but they have necessary information that helps the car understand the world it has to navigate. So a lot of effort has gone into incorporating this new type of data into solutions. These efforts have shown that HDMaps have remarkable benefits, both for fundamental problems like Object Detection and for precise trajectory forecasting problems.

However these maps are expensive to acquire and to maintain, because they need precise data acquisition and exacting human labeling. So there has been a strong push to approximate HDMaps from sensor data. Seminal work showed that even rough estimated maps are useful for trajectory forecasting.

Recent methods like MapTRv2 have become good at generating online HDMaps from raw sensors, but we think they overlook data that is very useful and nearly always available: existing maps. Our position is that outdated or lower quality maps should usually be available and that they significantly improve the estimated HDMaps, as shown in Fig. 1. In fact, even “map-free” models tend to use lower-quality satnav maps, and estimated maps could always be available if a vehicle went through a place once.

In this paper we explore the central postulate that even inaccurate existing maps improve the estimation of HDMaps from raw sensors. After giving some context on our method and the field in Sec. 2, we propose two separate technical contributions: in Sec. 3 we describe reasonable scenarios where an inaccurate map can be available, with practical implementations, and in Sec. 4 we propose MapEX, an architecture that generates HDMaps from sensor data while taking existing map information into account. Last, in Sec. 5 we present results with experiments on the nuScenes dataset.

Contributions The three contributions of this paper are:

- We propose to take existing map information into account when estimating online HDMaps from sensor data.

- We discuss reasonable scenarios where existing maps are not perfect. We also give realistic implementations of these scenarios and the code for the nuScenes dataset.

- We introduce MapEX, a new query based framework for HDMap estimation that can use existing map information when estimating an online HDMap from sensors. In particular, MapEX introduces a new way to use existing map information with non-learnable existing (EX) queries, and a way to make sure the model uses this information by pre-attributing predictions to known ground truth correspondences during training.

Impact We think these contributions are of real interest to the field because:

- MapEX greatly lowers the bar for getting good and cost-effective map estimations. For example, in one scenario where we use HDMaps with noisy (or “shifted”) map element positions, MapEX reaches 84.8% mAP, which is 38% better than the MapTRv2 detector it is built on. It is also 8% better than the state-of-the-art from MapNeXt, which uses a foundation model image backbone (while we use a ResNet-50 backbone). As estimated maps get more complex, MapEX will be more and more crucial for good and cost-effective performance.

- MapEX is the first method that directly integrates an existing map that corresponds exactly to the sensor data from the given location (i.e. the input sample) to guide online HDMap estimation. As far as we know this is a blind spot in the literature, where previous works only consider geolocalized satellite maps, SDMaps, or try to retrieve an existing map similar to the sample from a pre-computed database. None of these methods use sensor data to correct a flawed existing map.

- We give the implementation of existing map scenarios for online HDMap estimation for three realistic scenarios. Importantly, our implementations give both the (flawed) existing HDMaps and the true HDMap for every sample. This is not the case for the existing Trust but Verify map change detection dataset, which only gives the existing HDMap and a label saying whether a change happened.

Map nomenclature We work on local 30m\times 60m maps that are restricted to the surroundings of a sample. True maps are the ground truth maps, existing maps are the maps that are available as inputs, and predicted maps are the maps a model estimates.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous Driving [1,2] is a complex problem that promises to significantly change how we interact with transportation. While full vehicle automation still seems quite a ways away [3], partially autonomous vehicles now populate a number of road systems in the world [1]. These vehicles need to process a wealth of information to function, from raw sensor data [4] to elaborate maps of road networks [2,5].

High Definition maps (HDMaps), in particular, are a crucial component of research on self-driving cars [2,6] (see Fig. 1 for a few simple examples of maps, with road boundaries represented by green polylines, lane dividers by lime polylines and pedestrian crossings by blue polygons). Although maps are not a typical input of neural networks, they contain information the car needs to understand the world it must navigate. As such, significant efforts have gone into incorporating this new type of data into solutions [2,7]. These efforts have shown HDMaps’ remarkable benefits for problems ranging from fundamental ones like Object Detection [8] to precise trajectory forecasting [5,7].

These maps are, however, expensive to acquire and maintain, requiring precise data acquisition and exacting human labeling [6,9]. There has therefore been a strong push [10,11] to approximate HDMaps from sensor data. Seminal work [12] has shown that even rough estimated maps are useful for trajectory forecasting.

While recent methods like MapTRv2 [13] have become proficient at generating online HDMaps from raw sensors, we feel they overlook very useful and nearly always available data: existing maps. We posit that outdated or lower quality maps should usually be available and can significantly improve the estimated HDMaps, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Indeed, even “map-free” models tend to use lower-quality satnav maps [14], and estimated maps could always be available as long as a vehicle has gone through a place once.

In this paper, we explore the central postulate that even inaccurate existing maps improve the estimation of HDMaps from raw sensors. After providing some context on our method and the field in Sec. 2, we propose two distinct technical contributions: in Sec. 3, we outline reasonable scenarios under which an inaccurate map can be available, along with practical implementations, and in Sec. 4, we propose MapEX, an architecture that generates HDMaps from sensor data while accounting for existing map information. Finally, we present results in Sec. 5 with experiments on the nuScenes dataset [15].

Contributions We detail the following three contributions in this paper:

- We propose to account for existing map information when estimating online HDMaps from sensor data.

- We discuss reasonable scenarios under which existing maps are not perfect. We also provide realistic implementations of these scenarios and the code for the nuScenes dataset.

- We introduce MapEX, a new query based HDMap estimation framework that can incorporate existing map information when estimating an online HDMap from sensors. In particular, with MapEX we introduce both a novel way to incorporate existing map information through non-learnable existing (EX) queries, and a way to ensure the model uses this information by pre-attributing predictions to known ground truth correspondences during training.

Impact We believe these contributions are of substantial interest to the field because:

- MapEX drastically lowers the bar for obtaining good and cost-effective map estimations. In one scenario where we use HDMaps with noisy (or “shifted”) map element positions, for instance, MapEX reaches an 84.8% mAP score, an improvement of 38% over the MapTRv2 detector it is based on. This is also an 8% improvement over the state-of-the-art set by MapNeXt [16] with a foundation model image backbone [17] (vs. our ResNet-50 backbone). As estimated maps become more complex, MapEX will become increasingly crucial to good and cost-effective performance.

- MapEX is the first method to directly integrate an existing map corresponding precisely to the sensor data from the given location (i.e. the input sample) to guide online HDMap estimation. To the best of our knowledge, this is a blind spot of the literature, with previous works only considering geolocalized satellite maps [18], SDMaps [19,20], or trying to retrieve an existing map similar to the sample from a pre-computed database [21]. None of these methods use sensor data to correct a flawed existing map.

- We provide the implementation of existing map scenarios for online HDMap estimation following three realistic scenarios. Importantly, our implementations provide both the (flawed) existing HDMaps and the true HDMap for each sample. This is not the case for the existing Trust but Verify [22] map change detection dataset, which only provides the existing HDMap and a label indicating whether a change has occurred.

Map nomenclature We work on local 30m\times 60m maps restricted to a sample’s surroundings. True maps are the ground truth maps, existing maps are the maps available as inputs, and predicted maps are the maps estimated by a model.
